title: "Managing speaker and recording metadata"

  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Managing speaker and recording metadata}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(reindeer)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
src <- demo_corpus()@basePath
work <- tempfile("meta_"); dir.create(work); file.copy(src, work, recursive = TRUE)
corp <- corpus(file.path(work, basename(src)))
```

Metadata is stored in plain `METADATA.json` files next to the data they
describe: one in the corpus directory, one per session, one per bundle. Those
files are the ground truth; the corpus's SQLite cache is rebuilt from them.

## Three levels, most specific wins

```{r levels}
set_metadata(corp, list(Project = "Demo study", Country = "SE"))        # whole corpus
set_metadata(corp, list(Age = 31, Gender = "Female"), session = "0000") # one session
set_metadata(corp, list(Quality = "poor"),
             session = "0000", bundle = "msajc010")                     # one bundle
get_metadata(corp) |> select(bundle, Project, Age, Gender, Quality)
```

Reading resolves the inheritance for you: every bundle shows the
corpus-wide `Project`, the session's `Age` and `Gender`, and its own
`Quality` where one was set. Writing validates against the metadata schema
before touching a file, and keeps the cache in step.

## From a table

A data frame sets many scopes in one go and is checked as a whole first: if
one row names a bundle that does not exist, nothing is written.

```{r table}
speakers <- data.frame(
  session = "0000",
  bundle  = c("msajc003", "msajc010", "msajc012"),
  Speaker = c("P01", "P02", "P03")
)
set_metadata(corp, speakers)
get_metadata(corp) |> select(bundle, Speaker) |> head(4)
```

```{r bad}
tryCatch(
  set_metadata(corp, data.frame(session = "0000", bundle = c("msajc015", "nope"), Rating = 1:2)),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

Values keep their type: numbers stay numeric, dates are stored as ISO-8601
text, and a field that holds both integers and decimals is numeric across the
corpus.

## Edit in a spreadsheet and come back

`export_metadata()` writes a workbook with one sheet each for bundles,
sessions and the database. It contains the raw value at each level (not the
inherited ones), so importing it again changes nothing you did not edit.

```{r excel, eval = requireNamespace("openxlsx", quietly = TRUE)}
xlsx <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
export_metadata(corp, xlsx)
openxlsx::getSheetNames(xlsx)

# ... edit the file in Excel, then:
set_metadata(corp, xlsx)       # the whole workbook is validated before any write
```

## Files edited outside R

Opening a corpus checks the modification time of every metadata file, so
edits made with a text editor or by a colleague are picked up automatically;
there is nothing to reload. A malformed file stops the sync with an error that
names it and leaves the previous cache untouched.

## Older files

A corpus that still has `<name>.meta_json` files is read as before. The first
time you write to a level, its legacy fields are carried over into
`METADATA.json`, which then takes precedence at that level.

## Clearing and the paper trail

`set_metadata(..., reset = TRUE)` clears the fields at a scope before
writing. After a write, reindeer regenerates the corpus's FAIR documentation
(see `vignette("archiving")`) when the metadata actually changed.
